title: Writing for buyers who skim
excerpt: Put the point in the first lines and in the headings. A buyer who only skims should still be able to repeat your offer from the page.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window. The hands at the keyboard fit a piece about writing a page a buyer can scan without missing the offer.
caption: The first lines have to carry the point. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How do you write for someone who will not read the whole page?
faqs.answer: Put the offer in the first lines and repeat the claims in the headings. A person who reads only those should be able to say what you do and what to do next. The paragraphs underneath are for the reader who stays. They should add proof and detail, not introduce the point for the first time.

faqs.question: Are short pages always better?
faqs.answer: No. A skim needs structure, not a shortage of information. A buyer with a real budget will read the section that answers their objection if the heading tells them it is there. Cutting the only proof, in the name of brevity, leaves the skimmer with a slogan and nothing to trust.

faqs.question: Where should the ask go?
faqs.answer: Near the top, once the offer is clear, and again after the proof. The first ask catches the person who is already convinced. The later ask catches the person who needed the middle of the page. Both should use the same words for the same action, so the page does not seem to offer two different next steps.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Put the point in the first lines and in the headings. That is scannable web writing. A buyer who never slows down should still be able to repeat the offer from the headings alone. The paragraphs are for the one who stays to check the details.

Nielsen Norman Group's summary of reading on the web is the constraint. On the pages people actually visit, they have time to read only about a quarter of the text. Visits are often over within 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is obvious fast, and the average visit lasts a little less than a minute. You are not writing for a captured audience. You are writing a page that can be understood in layers.

## The first lines carry the offer

The first sentence names the buyer and the job. The second says how to act, or what has to be true for the work to fit. Warm-up is expensive. "We believe in craft" can be true and still tell a stranger nothing. Move the belief under a claim they can test.

Write the way you would answer a founder who asked, on a short call, what you do. Then remove the throat-clearing you would have edited out of your own mouth. The homepage hero, the top of a service page, and the top of an article all owe that answer. The formats differ. The duty does not.

Do not hide the point under a logo animation, a full-bleed video, or a heading that is only a brand adjective. If the first readable text is late, the skimmer has already left, and they left without the sentence you were saving for a reveal. Reveals are for people who have agreed to stay. Agreement comes after the point.

Read the first two paragraphs out of context, the way a stranger will. If they could belong to any studio or any product in the category, they are not done. Specific is what survives a skim. The category word can be there. The particular offer has to be there too.

## Headings are a second article

A skimmer jumps from heading to heading and builds a story from those lines alone. Write them as claims. "What you receive in the first two weeks" is a heading. "Our process" is a label they can skip without losing information, because it never had any. The test is simple. Read only the headings, in order, and see if you can repeat the offer and the next step.

Keep the grammar parallel when the sections are a set. Three steps should sound like three steps. A set that mixes a noun, a question, and a slogan looks unsorted, and the eye cannot use it as a list. Parallel headings are a kindness to the scan path.

The heading must match the paragraph under it. A sharp heading followed by a soft, unrelated block is a broken promise, and it teaches the reader not to trust the next heading. If the paragraph is the real point, fix the heading. If the heading is the real point, rewrite the paragraph so the first sentence delivers it.

Do not use headings as a place for jokes the body then has to translate. The skim never sees the translation. Wit can live in a sentence. The heading's job is orientation. A person using find-in-page, or a screen reader jumping by heading, is using them as navigation. Vague navigation is a product defect.

## Lists when the reader is choosing

Use a list when the reader is comparing or checking. What is included. What is not. What you need from them before kickoff. What the page will not do. A list is scannable because each item is a unit. A paragraph that hides five conditions in commas is a list that is ashamed of itself.

Keep items short and in the same shape. Start with the thing, not with "we." If an item needs two sentences of exception, it is not an item. Give it a paragraph under a heading of its own. A list of twelve, with sub-bullets, has become a document no one skims. Split it or cut it.

Do not list adjectives. "Fast, flexible, premium, human" is not a list a buyer can use. They cannot tell if you are a fit. List decisions and deliverables. The adjective can modify a noun that means something. It should not be the whole line.

Numbers help when the order is real. A sequence of steps should be numbered. A set of equal options should be bullets. Mixing them at random makes the page look like it was pasted from notes. The notes were fine. The page has a reader who was not in the meeting where the notes made sense.

## Proof a skimmer can see

Proof has to be visible at skim speed. A logo they recognize, a one-line result with the situation named, a picture of the actual work, a short constraint you are willing to say out loud. Bury the proof in the fifth paragraph and the skimmer never meets it. Put a concrete fact high, then let the section earn the nuance.

Name the situation in any quote you use. A line that says the team was pleasant is invisible to a serious buyer. A line that says what changed, in which kind of project, can be judged. If you do not have that line yet, do not invent one. Show the work. A specific project is better proof than a vague compliment, and it skims cleanly if the caption says what the project is.

Links are part of the skim. The words of the link should say what the reader will get. "Selected work" tells them. "Click here" does not. They decide from the link text whether to leave the scan and go deeper. Write the link as a phrase you would be willing to see alone, because sometimes it will be.

Calls to action are headings in disguise. Repeat the same action in the same words. Two competing buttons, "Get started" and "Talk to sales" and "See a demo," force a decision about the decision. Pick the one next step for this page. A second path can be a text link for people who are not ready. It should not be a second hero.

## What to cut

Cut the sentence that restates the heading without adding a fact. Cut the company origin if it does not change the buying decision. Cut adjectives that any competitor could claim. Cut the paragraph you wrote to sound like a studio. The reader can hear it, and it does not help them choose.

Cut repeated points. Saying the work is careful in the hero, again in the values, and again in the footer, does not make it truer. Say it once, next to the evidence, and move on. Repetition feels like emphasis in a draft and like padding on a page. Skimmers notice padding as length, then leave.

Keep the sentence that a skeptical person would ask for. Price shape, timeline shape, what you will not take on, what they must provide, who owns the work at the end. Those sentences do not feel glamorous in a copy deck. They are the ones a buyer stops for. Put them under headings that announce them, so the skim can find them.

Read the page on a phone, out loud, standing up. Where you run out of breath, the sentence is too long for a skim. Where you lose the thread, a heading is missing or a paragraph started too late. Fix those spots before you polish vocabulary. Vocabulary is not the bottleneck. Structure is.

## A test with the headings only

Print the headings, or paste them into a blank note. Hand them to someone who knows the company and someone who does not. Ask what the page is offering and what they would do next. If the outsider cannot answer, the headings are labels or the offer is missing. If the insider says "well, the body explains," the body is doing a job the skim will never collect.

This test is also how you brief a writer or a studio. Bring the headings you want a stranger to remember. The design can make them visible. It cannot invent their meaning. A beautiful page with empty headings is a fast skim of nothing.

On a Hanabi page the headings are written as claims, the first lines answer them, and the action is the same at the top and the bottom. That is the structure a founder can maintain after launch, because it does not depend on a performance of prose. It depends on saying the thing.

When you want a site written so a busy buyer can repeat the offer, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current headings. The review starts by reading nothing else.

Headings are easy to leave as labels when a template suggests them. [Headings that are not labels](/blog/headings-that-are-not-labels) is the next piece, with the difference between "Our process" and a line that actually says what happens.
